---
title: "From canvas to page"
---

Last year you painted pixels. p5.js handed you one canvas, and your code drew
lines and circles onto it. This year the browser builds the page instead, out
of pieces called elements, and your TypeScript code talks to those pieces. Same
language, new world.

Before any of that gets explained, get a page running on your own computer.

## Get the starter project running {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-run}

This year's starter project is called
[vite-ts-starter](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter),
and it is the same idea as last year's p5.js starter: a prepared folder you
copy for every exercise. Work through these steps now.

1. Open the
   [vite-ts-starter repository](https://github.com/Teaching-HTL-Leonding/vite-ts-starter)
   on GitHub. Click the green **Code** button and choose **Download ZIP**. The
   **Use this template** button next to it makes your own copy of the project
   on GitHub, which is the better route once you work with git. Git gets its
   own chapter later in this book, so today the ZIP is the faster way in.
2. Unpack the ZIP into your course folder and rename the unpacked folder to
   `hello-page`. The folder rule from last year still holds: a short, plain
   path such as `C:\Code\creative-coding`, and nothing inside OneDrive or
   Dropbox.
3. Start VS Code, choose **File > Open Folder**, and open `hello-page`. Say
   yes when VS Code asks whether you trust the authors.
4. Open the integrated terminal and run `npm install`. It fetches the packages
   listed in `package.json` and answers with a line like
   `added 19 packages, and audited 20 packages in 865ms`.
5. Run `npm start`. The terminal prints the address of your own development
   server (version numbers may differ):

   ```text
     VITE v8.2.2  ready in 107 ms

     ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/
   ```

6. Open that address in your browser. A big heading says **Hello World!**

## Change the text and watch {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-change}

Leave the server running and open `src/index.ts`. The whole file is two lines
of code:

```ts
const helloWorldHeader = document.getElementById('helloWorldHeader') as HTMLHeadingElement;

helloWorldHeader.innerText += '!';
```

Change the text in the second line to your own name and save the file:

```ts
helloWorldHeader.innerText += ' from Lena!';
```

Do not switch to the browser and reload. Just look at it. The page has already
changed itself and now reads **Hello World from Lena!** That is the development
server watching your files, the same hot reload you had last year.

Now open `index.html`, the file next to `src`. Find this line:

```html
<h1 id="helloWorldHeader">Hello World</h1>
```

Replace `Hello World` with `My page` and save. The heading turns into **My page
from Lena!**

You just changed the same heading from two different files. Nothing here has
been explained: not the `<h1>` around the text, not the `id` on it, not
`getElementById`, and not the strange `as HTMLHeadingElement` at the end of the
first line. That is on purpose. The next chapters take this project apart, one
piece per chapter, and you will meet every one of those words again.

## What you know, what is new {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-new}

Most of your first year still counts. Here is what carries over and what
changes.

| From year one | This year |
|---|---|
| TypeScript with variables, loops, arrays, and functions | The same TypeScript, plus objects and classes you write yourself |
| p5.js painted shapes onto a canvas | The browser builds the page from HTML elements and CSS, and SVG draws the shapes |
| `draw()` ran 60 times per second | The page sits still until your code or a click changes it |
| p5.js called `mousePressed()` for you | You attach a listener to the one element that should react |
| Your program was a single `src/index.ts` | A project of several files that work together |
| VS Code, npm, and the Vite starter | The same tools, plus git and automated tests |

## How this book works {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-book}

**Experiments come first.** You just ran one. Every chapter opens with
something to type and watch, and the name for what happened comes afterwards.
Reading the explanation before you have seen the effect is the slower way
around.

**Research tasks are part of the course.** This book is not a reference, so it
names a thing and shows why it matters, then sends you out for the details.
Those spots are marked by a box titled **Research task**. The box asks three to
five questions, and the book will not answer them anywhere. You look them up on
MDN, with a search engine, or by asking an AI, and you write the answers down in
your own words. The exercise right after the box needs them.

Every research box belongs to a quiz, so you can let the quiz drive you. Read a
question, answer it if you can, research it if you cannot, and come back until
every question has an answer.

**Most chapters end with a quiz** on the novedu platform. You answer in your
own words, an AI reads your answers and tells you what is solid and what to
read again, and the whole thing is anonymous. German answers are fine. This
chapter has no quiz, because so far nothing has been explained.

## Two rules for the whole year {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-rules}

**The exam rule.** Exams happen on a computer, without internet and without
AI. The course material is allowed. So the question to ask yourself all year is
not whether you can find something, but whether you can rebuild it with only
this book and your own notes in front of you.

**The AI rule.** Use AI to get unstuck and to explain error messages you
have never seen before. Every line you hand in is a line you must be able to
explain out loud, and "the AI wrote it" is not an explanation. The next chapter
sets up a coding buddy that knows this course and stays at your level.

## Where you stand {#sec-from-canvas-to-page-done}

Your `hello-page` folder holds a real web page, served by your own development
server, with a heading that carries your name. Keep the folder. The next
chapter puts a coding buddy on your machine, and Part 2 then opens these same
two files and starts naming what is inside them.
